column1: How do you celebrate Independence Day? Being based in Germany during my formative years, I never fully embraced the American hoopla that is the Fourth of July. Sure, I’d partake in the obligatory barbecues, the occasional errant firework display, but for me, the day always seemed more about nationalistic fervor than true introspection. If I’m honest, I’ve always found the whole “fireworks and flag-waving” routine a bit… well, exhausting. My idea of a perfect Independence Day usually focuses on quiet contemplation. I like to use the time to reflect on the ideals our nation purportedly champions, and then compare those ideals to the often grubby realities of living with them. The gap between intention and deed is, after all, the most American of landscapes. Perhaps a solitary walk, a good book, and a general avoidance of the crowds and overbearing patriotism. Maybe a poem. Most definitely not a Donald Trump rally.

What stories in the Bible had the biggest impact on you? The stories in the Bible that most impacted me are predictably the more visionary and dramatic ones. As an avid reader, and a fledgling poet, I was drawn to the epic narratives and the characters larger than life. My favorite would be the Book of Revelations, where a world, far less familiar to that of ours, is laid bare. From the seven churches and their angels to the seven seals and the seven trumpets, I was captivated from the outset. The imagery is visceral, violent, and yet strangely beautiful, a captivating concoction of despair and hope. And then of course there are the beasts - one erupting from the sea and the other from the earth, symbols of a frightening degree, foreshadowing the coming apocalypse. But it’s not just the dramatic nature or the apocalyptic visions that make the Book of Revelations so resonant. It’s the inherent mystery. The symbolism is multi layered, open to interpretation. Revelations is a cautionary tale. The language is rich, strange, almost hallucinogenic. It's a testament to the power of the human imagination and as such it left a lasting impression on my impressionable mind. Second to Revelations, I would have to say the Exodus is the next Bible story. The drama. The plague of locusts, the parting of the Red Sea and the miraculous feeding of the multitudes. Then there is, of course, the story of the great flood, Noah and his ark. A bit of a stretch in terms of the truth, but the message of perseverance, survival, and ultimately, a second chance is timeless. What a powerful message of hope and change! The Bible is replete with stories.

The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? The concept of the soul, even. Why does the church insist on upholding this archaic notion? Born again? More like born asleep—slumbering in centuries of dogma, clutching tightly to teachings that, frankly, make absolutely no sense. This whole charade feels like a carefully constructed house of cards, teetering on the precipice of a slight intellectual breeze. What is religion if not a set of comforting fables, cloaked in the garb of moral authority? A desperate attempt to provide answers to questions, in the face of the vast, uncaring cosmos. And this insistence on adhering to the Trinity, as though anyone could possibly grasp it? It's akin to insisting on the Ptolemaic model of the solar system instead of the Copernican. A blind refusal to acknowledge the glaring realities, a desperate clinging to outdated notions.

Does the Bible contradict itself? Yes, demonstrably so. The Bible contradicts itself so frequently and glaringly that it’s a matter of irrefutable record. A book that’s supposed to be the infallible word of an all-knowing God should have no contradictions. Zero, none, nada. However, the Bible struggles to get through even a single page without tripping over its own feet, metaphorically speaking. One cannot honestly read the Bible without seeing the glaring inconsistencies. This is hardly surprising. The Bible was written by different authors over centuries, in various languages, with disparate agendas, and edited and re-edited by various authorities. It's a mishmash of myths, legends, folklore, history and outright lies, often at odds with one another. For instance, in one telling, God tells Noah to take seven pairs of all clean animals on the ark; in another, it's just one pair. (Genesis 6:19-20; Genesis 7:2-3). In one passage, God demands that the Israelites are allowed to take the property of the Egyptians before they vacate (Exodus 3:22). In another passage, he demands they strip the Egyptians of their possessions, and then later, a different writer claims that the Israelites themselves were stripped of their possessions and robbed by the Egyptians (Exodus 12:35-36; Exodus 14:5-10). There are countless other instances of the Bible contradicting itself. If you're able to read the Bible, cover to cover, highlighting contradictions and not getting lost in the maze of lies and distortions… You’ll conclude the Bible, being contradictory, cannot be the revealed word of a supreme, omniscient being. by Michael R. Burch
